entry.title: Pagination concept in OData - ECC for SP - 7.3
entry.content:
Summary

This technical blog will open option to include pagination concept in Odata Service running on ECC system.

Introduction

This article is specific for developer who are still developing Odata Services on ECC on Pagination Concept.

There are multiple blogs available  on Pagination on S4 system but eventually same concept or logical approach is challenging while working in the ECC system.

How pagination works in S4 HANA system

Will talk on the existing solutioning part on S4 end before we come to ECC.

There are two keywords being used to restrict the count - one is $top and the other is $skip.  Both of the them play roles to restrict the count. I will not go in details about their operations as there are already existing blogs on it.

In S4, above keywords are used in the follows syntax to perform Pagination.

 

      SELECT <field1>,
                  <field2>,
                  ...          ,
                  ...          ,
                 <fieldn>
          FROM <SAP DB table>
         ORDER by <Key_field>
         INTO TABLE @<internal_table>
        OFFSET @paging-skip UP TO @paging-top ROWS.
 
Challenge in ECC system
But when it comes to ECC, above syntax difficult to apply directly as SKIP & ROWS are being used with OFFSET and UPTO keywords, which are not applicable for SAP-ECC system.
 
Solution
But, there are other approaches to handle paging in ECC. Here instead of restricting at the time of data fetch using SELECT query, will narrate how paging can be used using SAP standard class.
Below steps to follow to implement pagination in ECC system.
1. Pull TOP & SKIP from IO_TECH_REQUEST_CONTEXT into work area.
2. Use PAGING Method of SAP Utility Class - /IWBEP/CL_MGW_DATA_UTIL.
3. Pass work area with TOP & SKIP in PAGING method.
 
Working Code is below
******************Data Declaration ***************************

DATA: WA_PAGING TYPE /IWBEP/S_MGW_PAGING.

******************Assign Top & Bottom***********************

WA_PAGING-TOP = IO_TECH_REQUEST_CONTEXT->GET_TOP( ).
WA_PAGING-SKIP = IO_TECH_REQUEST_CONTEXT->GET_SKIP( ).

****************Call Data Utility Class*************************
CALL METHOD /IWBEP/CL_MGW_DATA_UTIL=>PAGING
  EXPORTING
       IS_PAGING = WA_PAGING
  CHANGING
      CT_DATA = <ENTITY_SET>.  "This table can be EntitySet of Odata Service

 
Conclusion
CT_DATA will have only specific number of counts (Skip & Top) as specified in the URI.

entry.title: Enabling Background Job Execution in S/4HANA from Fiori Using CDS and OData
entry.content:
Business Scenario

Imagine a purchasing department needing to update material prices based on market conditions. Instead of manually running a report in background mode, users can select materials in a Fiori app and click “Update Prices”, which triggers a background job with selected data. 

Component Purpose

CDS ViewFor showing material list in Fiori
OData Function ImportTriggers a background job
Fiori AppAllows selection + button click
ABAP ReportExecutes price update logic
SM37Monitor the job execution

Step-by-Step Implementation 

Step 1: CDS View for Material Selection 

This will expose a simple material list for selection.

Step 2: Create SEGW Project and Import CDS View 

  • T-code: SEGW 
  • Create project: Z_MATERIAL_JOB_API 
  • Import CDS view as Entity Type 
  • Generate runtime artifacts 

Step 3: Add Function Import to SEGW 

  1. In SEGW: 
  1. Right-click Data Model → Function Imports → Create

  2.  

     Name: TRIGGER_PRICE_JOB 
  3. Return Type: None 
  4. HTTP Method: POST 

2. In Modeling, assign an Entity Set if needed (optional). 

Step 4: Implement Function Import Logic 

In class: ZCL_Z_MATERIAL_JOB_API_DPC_EXT 

method /iwbep/if_mgw_appl_srv_runtime~execute_action. 
 
  data: lv_jobname type tbtcjob value 'ZPRICE_UPDATE_JOB', 
        lv_jobcount type tbtco-jobcount, 
        lv_msg type string, 
        lt_materials type standard table of mara-matnr. 
 
  if iv_action_name = 'TRIGGER_PRICE_JOB'. 
 
    " (Optional) collect materials from CDS selection or payload 
    append 'MATERIAL1' to lt_materials. 
    append 'MATERIAL2' to lt_materials. 
 
    " Submit the job 
    call function 'JOB_OPEN' 
      exporting 
        jobname          = lv_jobname 
      importing 
        jobcount         = lv_jobcount 
      exceptions 
        others           = 1. 
 
    if sy-subrc = 0. 
      " Submit custom report in background 
      submit zmat_price_update_report 
        with so_matnr in lt_materials 
        user sy-uname 
        via job lv_jobname 
        number lv_jobcount 
        and return. 
 
      call function 'JOB_CLOSE' 
        exporting 
          jobname     = lv_jobname 
          jobcount    = lv_jobcount 
          strtimmed   = 'X' 
        exceptions 
          others      = 1. 
 
      lv_msg = |Job { lv_jobname } triggered successfully.|. 
 
    else. 
      lv_msg = 'Job could not be started.'. 
    endif. 
 
    " Send response back to OData 
    data: lr_return type ref to /iwbep/if_message_container. 
    lr_return = me->get_message_container( ). 
    lr_return->add_message( 
      exporting 
        iv_msg_text   = lv_msg 
        iv_msg_type   = /iwbep/if_message_container=>gcs_msg_type-success 
    ). 
 
  endif. 
 
endmethod.

Step 5: Background Report ZMAT_PRICE_UPDATE_REPORT

REPORT zmat_price_update_report. 
 
PARAMETERS: so_matnr TYPE mara-matnr RANGE. 
 
START-OF-SELECTION.	 
 
  LOOP AT so_matnr INTO DATA(lr). 
    " Dummy logic - Simulate price update 
    WRITE: / 'Updating price for material:', lr-low. 
  ENDLOOP.

Output – What Happens in Fiori

  1. User opens the Fiori app showing materials from CDS.

  2. Selects a few materials → clicks “Update Prices”.

  3. The TRIGGER_PRICE_JOB function import is called.

  4. SAP triggers a job: ZPRICE_UPDATE_JOB

  5. The custom report runs in background → check SM37

Log: 

Conclusion:

This approach bridges Modern UI and robust backend logic. You can now let Fiori apps initiate background-heavy tasks — like price updates, data migration, or batch jobs — with traceable and efficient execution.

entry.title: SITLON 2025 - Segurança em Aplicações/Serviços no BTP em épocas de IA, e toda sua história/evolução!
entry.content:
Hello World! Tudo bem?

Após o encerramento com sucesso do primeiro SAP Inside Track Londrina (2025), que foi um evento somente presencial e contou com muitas apresentações de qualidade, resolvi criar esse material aqui na comunidade para aqueles que não puderam comparecer pessoalmente. 

Então segue a apresentação do conteúdo do SIT Londrina 2025, em formato "Live":

Mas se ainda não se contextualizou, sugiro antes de assistir o material acima ler todo o conteúdo abaixo e entender a evolução até o evento SIT Londrina 2025, ok?

Se você não conhece SAP e chegou até aqui, segue um pequeno resumo:

SAP é um software de gestão empresarial usado pelas maiores e mais importantes empresas do mundo para integrar e otimizar processos de negócios cruciais, como finanças e logística. Ele centraliza dados para fornecer uma visão completa e em tempo real, permitindo decisões estratégicas mais rápidas e eficientes. A sua importância reside em ser uma espinha dorsal tecnológica que garante a eficiência e a competitividade global dessas corporações.

No evento, realizei a apresentação “Segurança em Aplicações/Serviços no BTP em épocas de IA” sobre Cyber Security no mundo SAP, para aplicações desenvolvidas em um modelo bem específico. Mas com esse post aqui, o objetivo é atingir e disponibilizar o conteúdo a todos da comunidade SAP, bem como os curiosos e interessados pelo tema de segurança da informação. Como muitos podem estar lendo pela primeira vez sobre o tema e o que eu já fiz até então, vou detalhar a historia desde o começo de uma maneira resumida até chegar no SIT Londrina 2025, ok?

Tudo começou na Pandemia, no ano de 2020/2021, onde estava fazendo uma pesquisa para um blog que iria escrever sobre um tutorial de um tipo desenvolvimento Web especifico (SAPUI5) . Esse tutorial seria sobre o desenvolvimento de aplicações UI5/FIORI ao publico B2C, ou seja usuários que em sua maioria nunca teriam visto nada sobre SAP e que para eles seria como uma aplicação Web qualquer, também aplicações essas que seriam disponibilizadas na internet para acesso do publico em geral. No Blog eu iria abordar a arquitetura recomendada, exemplos de códigos fonte, etc., porém na etapa de pesquisa para apresentar alguns “exemplos” já existentes no mercado, me deparei com cenários muito assustadores!

Para contextualizar, “o sistema SAP” sempre é em sua maioria um sistema “fechado”, onde o acesso é feito geralmente por quem de fato precisa do mesmo (até por questão de custo de licença). Analisando a minha experiencia, de colegas e muitos estudos, conseguia afirmar então que os profissionais que desenvolvem, desenham e/ou especificam soluções SAP ao “publico geral”, em sua maioria não tem uma preocupação com os quesitos de segurança. No mundo SAP, os desenvolvimentos geralmente ficam dentro do sistema e/ou na rede interna do cliente, então esse tópico nunca foi muito explorado pelos profissionais e consultorias que desenvolvem soluções customizadas, e esse aqui foi o principal motivador de iniciar todo o conteúdo. Ou seja, profissionais do mundo SAP precisam se atentar e se preparar ao criar soluções desse tipo, pois os impactos de não fazer algo correto podem ser enormes (que verá logo mais alguns exemplos). Pois se algum desses casos caísse nas mãos erradas, não só a imagem da empresa em questão que usa SAP, independente do país que está localizada, seria impactada com prejuízos financeiros e até implicações legais, mas nós profissionais do mundo SAP também seriamos impactados pela “imagem” que seria passada que o sistema SAP é de alguma maneira "inseguro".

Antes de entrarmos no detalhe tenho que falar algo importante, tudo que falarei daqui em diante diz respeito a aplicações/serviços customizados e não standard SAP, ou seja foram soluções desenvolvidas por alguém para atender o requisito daquele cliente em específico, e não algo que “vem” no produto SAP. Soluções SAP a nível de produto no geral são muitos seguras, onde a mesma investe muito para manter o mais alto nível de segurança, utilizando todas as ferramentas e métodos de mercado para tal. Até ter programas onde pode “contratar” profissionais de cyber segurança para tentar explorar e descobrir como deixar seus produtos mais seguros (onde eu posso ou não ter participado. NDA). Recomendo os links 1 e 2 para quem deseja se aprofundar mais no tema de segurança no nível de produto SAP. Outro ponto importante, é que demonstro como essas aplicações customizadas podem ser facilmente encontradas na internet por ferramentas como Google Buscador. 

Na pesquisa fui encontrando muitas empresas vulneráveis em um numero altíssimo, quase podendo afirmar que mais 30% das que encontrei, tinham algum problema. Então o que era um tutorial mudou para uma pesquisa mais aprofundada do tema, e com isso resolvi criar o movimento #SafeSAPUI5. Que basicamente iniciaria com a criação de material e conscientização dos profissionais para termos aplicações e serviços SAP seguros que estão expostos na internet. Pois aqui entra um detalhe técnico bem agravante, para muitos casos o requerimento do cliente (ou seja, o que ele precisa) é ter uma aplicação customizada porem sem ter a necessidade de nenhum tipo de autenticação por parte do usuário que vai acessar. Ou seja, ao clicar na URL ele já deve entrar na aplicação customizada e poder fazer a ação necessária, cenário esse que foge bem do “padrão” SAP e existem muitas e muitas aplicações como essa espalhadas pelo mundo.  

Os materiais do #SafeSAPUI5 podem ser encontrados aqui.

Além dos mesmos, como já estava pronto para escrever, resolvi criar um Ebook gratuito sobre o tema, juntando um pouco de historia, exemplos, dicas e casos reais. Com isso, nasceu o ebook UI5 Hacker, que pode ser encontrado gratuitamente aqui (Português e Inglês). 

Juntando tudo isso apresentei a primeira palestra do tema, ainda na Pandemia, no evento UI5 Con 2021 (em Inglês) que é a conferencia global de SAPUI5, biblioteca utilizada para realizar esses desenvolvimentos (mais detalhes na palestra ou ebook).

UI5CON 2021: #SafeSAPUI5: 

Depois da mesma, com a ajuda da própria SAP, consegui espalhar essa conscientização e também comunicar os clientes ao redor do mundo que estavam inseguros e foram citados nos exemplos da palestra e ebook (alguns com vulnerabilidades muito graves, como cópia do passaporte de todos os usuários pronta para ser extraída por exemplo). Importante, era possível conseguir isso sem precisar realizar nenhum tipo de hack, apenas saber executar um serviço/API que está exposto na internet (até pelo próprio navegador). 

Então em 2023, resolvi fazer um compilado do material de 2021 em Português (com alguns novos exemplos) e apresentar no SIT SP 2023 (Serviços Seguros & Aplicações Seguras), trazendo a tona novamente o material e o tema (agora focado mais em Português).

A palestra pode ser vista no Youtube aqui:

Com isso tive muitos feedbacks positivos de profissionais e de clientes SAP que resolveram suas vulnerabilidades e passaram a adotar as praticas em seu dia a dia, para esse e outros requisitos. Mas é importante falar, é possível SIM fazer uma aplicação WEB como essa que descrevi acima de maneira segura e protegida para o seu cliente, só seguir as boas praticas e utilizar as ferramentas corretas. Acontece que nesse "meio tempo", a adoção do SAP BTP (oferta da SAP de serviços Cloud, assim como os outros grandes players de tecnologia) cresceu exponencialmente no mundo todo. Se iniciou então um movimento de muitos clientes para levarem suas soluções para o BTP (conhecido como o movimento “move to cloud”), e alguns deles com aplicações se enquadrando nas possíveis vulnerabilidades descritas. 

Mas e então, apenas levar as aplicações ao BTP as deixam seguras? 

E com a chegada, popularização e massiva utilização/evolução das Inteligências Artificiais (IAs) impactam nisso tudo?

Para responder as questões acima e trazer a tona novamente o tema, resolvi criar o material da palestra apresentada no SIT Londrina 2025: “Segurança em Aplicações/Serviços no BTP em épocas de IA”. Mas como comentei antes, o evento foi somente presencial e por conta disso resolvi realizar uma “live” com o mesmo material e conteúdo para disponibilizar a todos o mesmo. Colocando em uma linha do tempo então, ficaria assim:

O PDF do material apresentado no SIT Londrina 2025 pode ser encontrado aqui.

Após a apresentação desse material (PDF e "Live"), demonstro que uma simples ida ao SAP BTP com aplicações nesse modelo não te deixará mais seguro. E com a chegada das IAs, existe hoje uma rápida revolução no segmento de Cyber Security (assim como o mundo em geral) que as empresas que utilizam soluções SAP devem estar atentas e preparadas. 

Espero que tenha gostado do conteúdo e lhe ajudado, e que de alguma maneira tenha agregando algo ao seu conhecimento atual. 

Obrigado e nos vemos nas próximas aventuras do “Hacker do Bem”.

entry.content:
Assuming that you have enabled the API Management capability in Integration Suite, I will start with API Provider creation.

1. Create API Provider

Authentication type
BASIC
Username
SAP's User Name for communication
Password
***

Test connection:

2. Create API Proxy

Select the API Provider, click on Discover to select the API which you wanted to use

Select the API & then click on Create.

3. Create Key Value Map to store the credentials to S/4HANA

 

4. Add Policies

Verify API Key - To verify the key which you are going to pass while calling the API.
Where do you get the API? - When you create the Product, and a Subscription, after creating a Subscription in the Developer Hub you will get a Key. That key is to be provided to the Consumer, and this Policy will verify the key sent by the consumer.

 <!--Specify in the APIKey element where to look for the variable containing the api key--> 
<VerifyAPIKey async='true' continueOnError='false' enabled='true' 
xmlns='http://www.sap.com/apimgmt'>
	<APIKey ref='request.header.apikey '/>
</VerifyAPIKey>

Key Value Map Operations - To fetch the credentials saved in the Key Value Mapping

<KeyValueMapOperations mapIdentifier="SAP_S4HANA_Credentials" async="true" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt">
    <Get assignTo="private.usernameFromKVM" index="1">
        <Key>
            <Parameter>Username</Parameter>
        </Key>
    </Get>
    <Get assignTo="private.passwordFromKVM" index="1">
        <Key>
            <Parameter>Password</Parameter>
        </Key>
    </Get>
    <Scope>environment</Scope>
</KeyValueMapOperations>

Basic Authentication - To pass the credentials fetched in the previous step.

<BasicAuthentication async='true' continueOnError='false' enabled='true' xmlns='http://www.sap.com/apimgmt'>
	<Operation>Encode</Operation>
	<IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>false</IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>
	<User ref='private.usernameFromKVM'></User>
	<Password ref='private.passwordFromKVM'></Password>
 	<AssignTo>request.header.Authorization</AssignTo>
</BasicAuthentication>

Assign Message - So you get an error as, "{"fault":{"faultstring":"Unsupported Encoding \"br\"","detail":{"errorcode":"protocol.http.UnsupportedEncoding"}}}". 
BR is a data format Brotli which is often defined by backend for webpage loading and not accepted by default. And this Assign Message will help your message reach the target.

<!-- This policy can be used to create or modify the standard HTTP request and response messages -->
<AssignMessage async="false" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" xmlns='http://www.sap.com/apimgmt'>
 
	<!-- Sets a new value to the existing parameter -->
	<Set>
		<Headers>
		     <Header name="Accept-Encoding">gzip,deflate</Header>
	     </Headers> 
	</Set>
	<IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>false</IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>
	<AssignTo createNew="false" type="request"></AssignTo>
</AssignMessage>

5. Create Product & Add the API

6. Create a Subscription for the Product created

7. It's time to test!

entry.title: Hands-On Guide: SAP Build + Joule Skill for Purchase Order Listing, Approval, or Modification
entry.content:
Introduction

In this tutorial, we will build an AI powered Purchase Order listing, modification or approval app using SAP Build and Joule. This step by step guide covers everything from OData integration to creating a working Joule Skill.

 

Table of Contents

  • 1. Create an Environment
  • 2. Exposing the Destination
  • 3. Create a database table to store purchase orders
  • 4. Create a CDS from the ZTABLE for Odata
  • 5. Create OData service with T-code SEGW
  • 6. Activate the Odata service via /iwfnd/maint_service T-code
  • 7. Crete an Action in SAP Build
  • 8. Create A Joule Skill to Get Purchase Order
  • 9. Create A Joule Skill to Approve Purchase Order
  • 10. Launch The Joule and Test The Skills

 

 

In today’s SAP ecosystem, intelligent automation is an expectation, not a future goal. SAP Build allows developers to quickly create business applications without extensive coding and SAP Joule brings AI-driven intelligence to these experiences.

In this hands-on guide, I’ll walk you through the process of building a Joule skill that connects to an OData service, allowing users to list, approve, and update purchase orders directly through SAP Build. ( This guide uses ZTABLE to store purchase order data because the standard SAP tables in the test system I work on don't have enough or the right kind of data. However, you can use the standard tables instead of ZTABLE. )

This project shows how AI capabilities can seamlessly integrate into SAP’s low-code environment, enabling automation and human decision-making in one interface. Whether you want to enhance your workflow with intelligent actions or explore real-world Joule integration scenarios, this guide will provide a practical starting point.

 

1. Create an Environment

 

We need to create an environment for testing joule skill.

Open the SAP Build Lobby, choose Control Tower->Environments and press the Create button.

 

 

Name your environment and add Description.

 

2. Exposing the Destination

 

Url of the destination on BTP is the url of our SAP system and the destination must have these properties: 

sap.applicationdevelopment.actions.enabled -> true

sap.processautomation.enabled -> true

sap.build.usage -> odata_gen

 

Also the destination’s user will be used for set an external break-point for debugging the ABAP code.

 

 

Open the SAP Build Lobby, choose Control Tower->Destinations and press the Add button.

 

Select the Destination and choose next.

 

Choose the environment in which you want to use the target. For this tutorial you can choose the Test Environment that you create.

 

3. Create a database table to store purchase orders

@EndUserText.label : 'Purchase Order Change With Sap Build'
@AbapCatalog.enhancementCategory : #NOT_CLASSIFIED
@AbapCatalog.tableCategory : #TRANSPARENT
@AbapCatalog.deliveryClass : #A

  key purchaseorder              : ebeln not null;

  material                       : matnr;
  materialcompisvariablesized    : boolean;
  materialcomponentisphantomitem : boolean;
  reservation                    : char10;
  @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure : 'zbg_build_test.entryunit'
  requiredquantity               : menge_d;
  requirementdate                : dats;
  reservationisfinallyissued     : boolean;
  baseunit                       : meins;
  @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure : 'zbg_build_test.entryunit'
  quantityinentryunit            : menge_d;
  entryunit                      : meins;
  plant                          : werks_d;
  latestrequirementdate          : dats;
  billofmaterialitemnumber       : ebelp;
  bomitemcategory                : char1;
  isbulkmaterialcomponent        : boolean;
  debitcreditcode                : shkzg;
  @Semantics.quantity.unitOfMeasure : 'zbg_build_test.entryunit'
  withdrawnquantity              : menge_d;
  approver                       : uname;
  appoved                        : flag;

}

 

Fill the table:

 

 

4. Create a CDS from the ZTABLE for Odata

 

@AbapCatalog.sqlViewName: 'ZSLV_BUILD_TST_V'

{   @EndUserText.label: 'Purchase Order'
    key purchaseorder,

}

 

5. Create OData service with T-code SEGW

(Because of the version of the system I work on, this guide uses SEGW instead of RAP to create an OData service. However, you can easily create your own OData service with RAP.)

Press ‘Create Project’ button, fill the fields and assign the package, request (For this tutorial it will be local object).

 

Complete the creation.

 

Extend the project, right click to ‘Data Model’, select the Reference->Source

 

 

Fill the CDS name that you created. Choose ‘Next’.

 

 

Choose ‘Finish’.

 

 

Activate and generate the Service:

 

 

Go to the class ZCL_ZSLV_BUILD_DPC_EXT. At the bottom of the method list redefine the update method ZSLV_V_BUILD_TES_UPDATE_ENTITY.

 

 

In the method, update the approved field with the below code and activate it.

 

METHOD zslv_v_build_tes_update_entity.
 
  DATA: lv_ebeln TYPE ebeln,
        lv_ebelp TYPE ebelp,
        lv_item  TYPE ebelp,
        ls_entity TYPE zcl_zslv_build_mpc=>ts_zslv_v_build_testtype,
        lr_entity TYPE REF TO data,
        ls_table TYPE zbg_build_test.
 
  LOOP AT it_key_tab INTO DATA(ls_key).
    CASE ls_key-name.
      WHEN 'purchaseorder'.
        lv_ebeln = ls_key-value.
      WHEN 'purchaseorderitem'.
        lv_ebelp = ls_key-value.
      WHEN 'reservationitem'.
        lv_item = ls_key-value.
    ENDCASE.
  ENDLOOP.
 
  io_data_provider->read_entry_data( IMPORTING es_data = ls_entity ).

entry.content:
Introduction

This blog post explains how to test OAuth-enabled inbound communication in SAP using an API client. It walks through the configuration steps and provides practical examples for validating the setup.

When working with inbound communication in SAP S/4HANA Cloud or on-premises systems, developers and integration specialists often need a lightweight tool to test APIs secured with OAuth 2.0.

While there are many API testing tools available today, this guide focuses on Bruno—a modern, open-source similar to the more established Postman. Personally I think of Postman as the old guard, and Bruno as the new pup on the block: sleek, efficient, and eager to fetch your tokens! (And yes, my love for dogs may have influenced this choice just a little.) 
                                                                         

Image was created by the author using an AI illustration tool and is original content.

 🐾 In this post, I’ll walk you through how to:

  1. Configure a custom communication arrangement based on an existing communication scenario for OAuth 2.0
  2. Use an API client to test inbound communication secured with OAuth 2.0

Note: This guide assumes you already have a communication scenario that supports OAuth 2.0.

Prerequisites

  • A communication scenario in your S/4HANA system that supports OAuth 2.0
  • An API client installed on your operating system (for example, Bruno, Postman, or any equivalent tool)

So, grab your treats and let’s get our paws dirty—Bruno’s ready to sniff out those OAuth tokens and help you unleash smoother integrations!

Step 1: Enable a Custom Communication Arrangement for OAuth

1. Create a Communication System and Communication User

🐾 Think of the Communication System as Bruno’s doghouse—it needs to be cozy, secure, and ready for visitors. 🐾

Open the Communication Systems app and create a new system:

System IDZ_BRUNO
System NameZ_BRUNO


Under Technical Data:

  1. Enable Inbound Only.
  2. In OAuth 2.0 Settings: 
    • Set Client Redirect URI Type to Loopback
    • Set a path in the Path field, e.g., /bruno/redirect
          → This becomes your Callback URL:   http://127.0.0.1/bruno/redirect (used in Step 2)

🐾 When you set the redirect path to /bruno/redirect, you’re basically telling Bruno where to wag his tail when he’s done fetching the token. 🐾

Under Users for Inbound Communication

  1.  Add a new communication user
  2.  Set Authentication Method to OAuth 2.0
  3.  Define OAuth 2.0 Client ID, e.g., Z_BRUNO_ID
  4. Enable Refresh Allowed and set Refresh Token Expiry Time, e.g., 5 Days

Save your communication system and inbound communication user for your future testing with Bruno acting as OAuth client. This user will be later used for the Authorization Code Grant with PKCE.

2. Create a Communication Arrangement

Open the Communication Arrangements app and create a new arrangement based on a communication scenario that supports OAuth 2.0 as an authentication method, e.g., SAP_COM_0053 (Purchase Order Integration).

Arrangement NameTEST_COM_0053_WITH_BRUNO
Communication System Z_BRUNO (defined earlier)

Under Inbound Communication:

 

  1. Enter the OAuth 2.0 Client ID you defined earlier: Z_BRUNO_ID.
  2. Save your communication arrangement.

Note: Only after saving the arrangement, the previously defined OAuth client gets actually created. A clickable label OAuth 2.0 Details will apear.

In OAuth 2.0 Details, you will find all the necessary data for your API client:

  1. Client ID
  2. Token Service URL
  3.  Authorization URL

These are needed to fetch a token with Bruno.

Now you are ready to test your OAuth-secured API using Bruno!


Step 2: Use Bruno to Test the OAuth Communication

🐾  Creating a new collection in Bruno is like giving your dog a new toy—name it, set it up, and let the fun begin!  🐾

  2. Create a New Collection
  3. Name it, e.g., My_test_collection

2. Set Up OAuth in the Auth Tab

  1. Go to the Auth tab and choose OAuth 2.0
  2. Set up the configurations:

3. Send a Test Request

  2. A browser window will open -  logon as a Business User

it likely means the user lacks the required authorizations or the wrong user was used.

Summary

With this setup, you can securely test OAuth-protected endpoints in SAP using Bruno or similar tools. This approach is useful for validating integration scenarios and troubleshooting authentication issues.

Bruno provides a clean and open-source alternative to Postman for testing OAuth-secured APIs in SAP S/4HANA. With just a few configuration steps, you can simulate real-world OAuth flows and validate your communication scenarios with ease.

🐾 With Bruno by your side, testing OAuth APIs is less of a chore and more of a walk in the park. Just don’t forget the treats (a.k.a. access tokens)! 🐾

A Comprehensive Guide to Extending SAP S/4HANA with the SAP Extensibility Wizard — Without Compromising Your Clean Core

Introduction

Extensibility is a critical aspect of SAP S/4HANA, enabling organizations to tailor the system to their unique business needs while maintaining stability and upgrade readiness. In this guide, we will explore the SAP Extensibility Wizard, a powerful tool designed to help developers extend SAP S/4HANA in a clean and controlled way.

What Is the SAP Extensibility Wizard?

The SAP Extensibility Wizard is a guided tool provided by SAP that simplifies the process of creating extensions. It ensures that developers can add custom functionality without modifying the core system, thereby preserving the clean core principle. This approach guarantees that upgrades remain smooth and that the system stays resilient over time.

Availability: Public Cloud vs. Private Cloud

A common question arises: Is the SAP Extensibility Wizard available only in the Public Cloud, or also in the Private Cloud?

  • Public Cloud (SAP S/4HANA Cloud – Public Edition):
    The wizard is primarily available here. It supports clean-core extensibility and helps organizations build safe, upgrade‑friendly extensions.
  • Private Cloud / On‑Premise:
    Extensibility is possible through other approaches such as in‑app extensibility, ABAP Cloud, and side‑by‑side extensions on SAP BTP. However, the wizard itself is not provided in the same way as in the Public Cloud.

In summary:

  • Public Cloud → Wizard available.
  • Private Cloud / On‑Premise → Extensibility options exist, but without the wizard.

Focus of This Blog

This blog will focus on the SAP Extensibility Wizard for SAP S/4HANA Cloud – Public Edition.

How to Use the Extensibility Wizard

With the SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition extensibility wizard, developers can:

  • Create on‑stack extensions such as custom fields and custom logic.
  • Build side‑by‑side extensions like custom processes using SAP Build Process Automation.

This guided approach ensures that extensions are implemented efficiently, securely, and in alignment with SAP’s clean‑core strategy.

Conclusion

The SAP Extensibility Wizard is a key enabler for organizations running SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. By leveraging this tool, businesses can extend their systems with confidence, ensuring that customizations remain upgrade‑safe and future‑proof.

Conclusion

The SAP Extensibility Wizard empowers organizations running SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition to extend their systems safely and efficiently, without compromising the clean core. By leveraging guided tools for custom fields, logic, and side‑by‑side processes, businesses can innovate while staying upgrade‑ready.

Extensibility in SAP is not just about adding features—it’s about doing so in a way that keeps your system future‑proof. With the wizard, you can confidently build the extensions your business needs today, while ensuring smooth upgrades tomorrow.

entry.title: How to Create a ServiceNow Incident via REST API Using ABAP (OAuth 2.0)
entry.content:
Prerequisites

  • ServiceNow instance access with API credentials (Client ID, Client Secret)
  • SAP NetWeaver with HTTP Client (CL_HTTP_CLIENT) and JSON support (/UI2/CL_JSON)

Step 1: Obtain OAuth2 Token from ServiceNow

First, you need to POST your client credentials to ServiceNow’s /oauth_token endpoint to get a bearer token. This token authorizes subsequent API calls.

ABAP Code:

FORM get_servicenow_token USING iv_token_url TYPE string
                              iv_client_id TYPE string
                              iv_client_secret TYPE string
                         CHANGING cv_token TYPE ty_token
                                  cv_errmsg TYPE string.

  DATA: lv_payload     TYPE string,
        lo_http_client TYPE REF TO if_http_client,
        lv_response    TYPE string,
        lt_token       TYPE STANDARD TABLE OF ty_token,
        lo_json        TYPE REF TO /ui2/cl_json.

  CLEAR: cv_errmsg, cv_token.

  lv_payload = |grant_type=client_credentials&client_id={ iv_client_id }&client_secret={ iv_client_secret }|.

  CALL METHOD cl_http_client=>create_by_url
    EXPORTING
      url    = iv_token_url
    IMPORTING
      client = lo_http_client
    EXCEPTIONS
      OTHERS = 1.

  IF sy-subrc <> 0 OR lo_http_client IS INITIAL.
    cv_errmsg = 'Failed to create HTTP client for token.'.
    EXIT.
  ENDIF.

  lo_http_client->request->set_method( 'POST' ).
  lo_http_client->request->set_header_field( name = 'Content-Type' value = 'application/x-www-form-urlencoded' ).
  lo_http_client->request->set_cdata( lv_payload ).

  TRY.
      lo_http_client->send( ).
      lo_http_client->receive( ).
      lv_response = lo_http_client->response->get_cdata( ).
      lo_http_client->close( ).
      CONCATENATE '[' lv_response ']' INTO lv_response.

      CREATE OBJECT lo_json.
      lo_json->deserialize( EXPORTING json = lv_response CHANGING data = lt_token ).
      IF lt_token IS NOT INITIAL.
        READ TABLE lt_token INDEX 1 INTO cv_token.
      ELSE.
        cv_errmsg = 'Could not parse token from JSON.'.
      ENDIF.
    CATCH cx_root INTO DATA(lx_err).
      cv_errmsg = lx_err->get_text( ).
  ENDTRY.
ENDFORM.

If successful, the access_token can now be used as a Bearer token.

Step 2: Build the JSON Payload

Create a JSON structure that describes the incident.

ABAP Code:

lv_json_body =
'{' &&
'"caller_id":"ABC Corp",' &&
'"service_offering":"SAP Material",' &&
'"category":"Data",' &&
'"subcategory":"Incorrect Data",' &&
'"short_description":"Test Incident from SAP",' &&
'"description":"Test Incident from SAP",' &&
'"impact":"2",' &&
'"urgency":"2"' &&
'}'.

Step 3: Create the Incident via POST API

Now, make a POST request to the ServiceNow incident table, including your access token for authorization.

ABAP Code:

FORM create_servicenow_incident
  USING iv_post_url TYPE string
        iv_access_token TYPE string
        iv_body TYPE string
  CHANGING cv_result TYPE string
           cv_errmsg TYPE string.

  DATA: lo_http_client TYPE REF TO if_http_client.

  CLEAR: cv_errmsg, cv_result.

  CALL METHOD cl_http_client=>create_by_url
    EXPORTING
      url    = iv_post_url
    IMPORTING
      client = lo_http_client.

  lo_http_client->request->set_method( 'POST' ).
  lo_http_client->request->set_header_field( name = 'Content-Type' value = 'application/json' ).
  lo_http_client->request->set_header_field( name = 'Accept' value = 'application/json' ).
  lo_http_client->request->set_header_field( name = 'Authorization' value = |Bearer { iv_access_token }| ).
  lo_http_client->request->set_cdata( iv_body ).

  TRY.
      lo_http_client->send( ).
      lo_http_client->receive( ).
      cv_result = lo_http_client->response->get_cdata( ).
      lo_http_client->close( ).
    CATCH cx_root INTO DATA(lx_err).
      cv_errmsg = lx_err->get_text( ).
  ENDTRY.
ENDFORM.

If successful, cv_result will contain the incident response from ServiceNow.

Step 4: Combine the Steps in Your Report

Your main program calls these subroutines in sequence.

Example Main Logic:

* Get the access token
PERFORM get_servicenow_token
               USING lv_token_url
                     lv_client_id
                     lv_client_secret
               CHANGING ls_token
                     lv_err.

IF lv_err IS NOT INITIAL OR ls_token-access_token IS INITIAL.
  WRITE: / 'Token Error:', lv_err.
  EXIT.
ENDIF.

* Create the incident
PERFORM create_servicenow_incident
                    USING lv_post_url
                          ls_token-access_token
                          lv_json_body
                   CHANGING lv_result
                            lv_err.

IF lv_err IS INITIAL.
  WRITE: / 'Incident Response:', lv_result.
ELSE.
  WRITE: / 'Incident Creation Error:', lv_err.
ENDIF.

Final Notes

  • Security: Never hardcode sensitive data in productive programs—use secure storage.
  • Error Handling: Always add robust error handling and log failures for troubleshooting.
  • Data Mapping: Adjust JSON fields based on ServiceNow table and your organization’s requirements.

Conclusion

Integrating SAP and ServiceNow allows you to automatically manage ITSM incidents directly from SAP ABAP.  The above example demonstrates OAuth token retrieval and incident creation using ABAP.  Adapt and build on this foundation to suit your business requirements.

Happy Integrating! Let me know in the comments if you have any questions or need clarification on any step.

*& Report ZSNOW
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*
* Utility: ServiceNow Incident API Integration
*---------------------------------------------------------------------*

TYPES: BEGIN OF ty_token,
         access_token TYPE string,
         scope        TYPE string,
         token_type   TYPE string,
         expires_in   TYPE i,

* Prepare JSON Body

entry.title: Building an Email-Based SAP Sales Order Automation with n8n & AI Function Calling
entry.content:
Building an Email-Based SAP Sales Order Assistant with AI Function Calling

The Problem That Started This

A few weeks ago, I was watching a colleague struggle with a simple request: "Can you check if order 10850 shipped?" They had to VPN in, open SAP GUI, navigate to VA03, enter the order number, and finally get the answer. For one question. That took 3 minutes.

I thought - what if they could just send an email and get an answer back?

Why Not Just Use Rules or Keywords?

My first instinct was simple pattern matching. Look for "create order" then run the create flow. Look for "check status" then run the query flow. Easy, right?

Then I looked at actual emails people send:

  • "Hey, can you set up an order for 17100003? They need 5 of TG11 and 10 of TG12"
  • "pls make SO for cust 17100003 - TG11 x5, TG12 x10"
  • "Customer 17100003 wants to place an order. Materials: TG11 (5 units), TG12 (10 units)"

Same request, completely different wording. Building regex patterns for every variation? That's a maintenance nightmare waiting to happen. And what about typos, abbreviations, or when someone writes in a mix of languages?

This is exactly where AI shines - understanding intent regardless of how it's expressed.

Why Function Calling Instead of Free-Form AI?

I didn't want the AI making up SAP field names or guessing at API structures. That's a recipe for errors. Function calling gives you the best of both worlds:

  • The AI handles the messy, unpredictable part (understanding what the user wants)
  • The code handles the precise, structured part (calling SAP correctly)

You define exactly what functions exist and what parameters they accept. The AI picks the right function and extracts the right values. No hallucinated field names, no invented API calls.

The Architecture

Four components working together:

  1. Microsoft Outlook - Triggers when an email arrives
  2. LLM with Function Calling - Interprets the email, picks the operation
  3. n8n - Orchestrates everything, handles data transformation
  4. SAP S/4HANA OData APIs - Does the actual work

 

Setting Up n8n with Docker (The Network Gotchas)

I run n8n locally in Docker, and connecting it to an on-premise SAP system over VPN was... an adventure. Here's what I learned.

The Basic Setup

docker run -it --rm \
  --name n8n \
  -p 5678:5678 \
  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  -v n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n \
  docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n

That --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway flag is crucial. It lets containers reference your host machine's network. Without it, your container is isolated and can't see anything your host can see - including VPN connections.

The VPN Problem

Here's the thing: when you connect to a VPN on your Mac, the VPN routes are available to your host machine, but Docker containers live in their own network namespace. They can't directly reach 172.16.0.11:44300 even though your browser can.

You might think "just use --network host" - but on macOS, that doesn't work the way you'd expect. Docker Desktop on Mac runs containers in a Linux VM, so --network host gives you the VM's network, not your Mac's network.

The socat Bridge Solution

The workaround is to run a TCP forwarder on your host that bridges the connection:

socat TCP-LISTEN:15001,fork,reuseaddr TCP:172.16.0.11:44300

This listens on port 15001 on your Mac and forwards traffic to the SAP server at 172.16.0.11:44300. Now from inside Docker, you can reach SAP at:

https://host.docker.internal:15001/sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SALES_ORDER_SRV/A_SalesOrder

The flow is: Docker container → host.docker.internal:15001 → socat on your Mac → VPN → SAP server

Keep the socat command running in a terminal while you're working. Kill it when you're done.

Quick Tip: If you're getting "connection refused" errors, check that:

  1. Your VPN is connected
  2. socat is running
  3. You're using host.docker.internal, not localhost or the direct IP

The Functions I Defined

Three operations cover most daily requests:

get_sales_orders

"Show me recent orders," "What's the status of order X?"

Parameters: $top, $filter, $orderby

create_sales_order

"Create an order for customer X with these items"

Parameters: SoldToParty, items[] (Material, RequestedQuantity), plus optional fields

update_sales_order

"Change the PO reference on order 10904"

Parameters: SalesOrder (required), plus any fields to update

When an email comes in, the AI returns structured JSON:

{
  "function": "create_sales_order",
  "arguments": {
    "SoldToParty": "17100003",
    "items": [
      {"Material": "TG11", "RequestedQuantity": "5"},
      {"Material": "TG12", "RequestedQuantity": "10"}
    ]
  }
}

Clean, predictable, easy to work with.

The CSRF Token Headache

I have to mention this because it cost me hours. SAP OData APIs require CSRF tokens for write operations. Sounds simple - fetch a token, send it with your POST. But here's what the documentation doesn't make obvious:

The token is tied to your session cookies. You need to:

  1. GET request with x-csrf-token: fetch header
  2. Capture the token AND the SAP_SESSIONID cookie from the response
  3. Send BOTH with your write request

I kept getting "CSRF token validation failed" with a perfectly valid token. Turns out I was missing the session cookie. The token alone is useless without it.

Another gotcha in n8n

The cookie header comes back with extra metadata like path=/; secure; HttpOnly. If you pass that whole string in your Cookie header, you'll get "Invalid character in header content." You need to extract just the cookie value:

// In an Edit Fields node, clean the cookie
$json.headers['set-cookie'][0].split(';')[0] + '; ' + 
$json.headers['set-cookie'][1].split(';')[0]

This gives you a clean sap-usercontext=sap-client=100; SAP_SESSIONID_S4H_100=abc123... that SAP will accept.

 

Data Transformation for Deep Insert

One more SAP quirk: when creating an order with line items, you can't just send an items array. SAP expects a nested structure called to_Item.results. In n8n's Code node:

const args = JSON.parse(
  $input.first().json.choices[0].message.tool_calls[0].function.arguments
);
const body = { ...args };

if (body.items) {
  body.to_Item = { results: body.items };
  delete body.items;
}

return [{ json: { sapBody: body } }];

This transforms the AI's clean output into SAP's expected format.

 

A Real Example

Input Email

Hello, please create a sales order with the following details:
Customer: 17100003
Sales Org: 1710
Items: TG11 (qty 5), TG12 (qty 10)
Currency: USD

What Happens

  1. AI identifies this as create_sales_order
  2. Extracts: customer, items array, currency
  3. Workflow fetches CSRF token + session cookie
  4. Transforms items array to SAP's to_Item.results format
  5. POSTs to /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SALES_ORDER_SRV/A_SalesOrder
  6. SAP creates order, returns details

Response Email

The user never touched SAP. They just sent an email.

What's Next

The same pattern works for anything with an OData API:

  • Invoice queries
  • Delivery status checks
  • Material lookups
  • Customer master updates

Define the function, connect the endpoint, done.

The Takeaway

AI isn't replacing SAP knowledge here - it's translating between human language and system requirements. The business logic, the validations, the actual processing - that's all still SAP. The AI just makes it accessible to people who don't speak SAP.

And honestly? That's the kind of AI use case I find most valuable. Not replacing expertise, but removing friction.

entry.title: How to Create an Application Job (APJ) in SAP S/4HANA ABAP — With Single Values & Select Options
entry.content:
This post covers end-to-end implementation of an Application Job using IF_APJ_RT_EXEC_OBJECT and IF_APJ_DT_EXEC_OBJECT interfaces, including both Single Value parameters and Select Option parameters.

What is an Application Job?

Application Jobs (APJ) are the modern replacement for classic SM36/SM37 background jobs in S/4HANA. They run via class-based execution and support proper parameter definition through the ADT (Eclipse) framework.

Step 1 — Create the Class

Your class must implement two interfaces:

  • IF_APJ_RT_EXEC_OBJECT — Runtime execution
  • IF_APJ_DT_EXEC_OBJECT — Design-time parameter definition
 
 
abap
CLASS zcl_my_apj_job DEFINITION
  PUBLIC FINAL
  CREATE PUBLIC.

  PUBLIC SECTION.
    INTERFACES:
      if_oo_adt_classrun,
      if_apj_rt_exec_object,
      if_apj_dt_exec_object.

    " Single value parameter constants
    CONSTANTS: gv_date TYPE char8  VALUE 'SnapDate',
               gv_lang TYPE char5  VALUE 'LANGUAGE',
               gv_uom  TYPE char5  VALUE 'UOM'.

    " Select option parameter constants
    CONSTANTS: gv_contracttype TYPE char10 VALUE 'SO_CON',
               gv_compcode     TYPE char10 VALUE 'SO_COMP',
               gv_plant        TYPE char10 VALUE 'SO_Plant'.

ENDCLASS.

Step 2 — GET_PARAMETERS : Single Values

 
 
abap
METHOD if_apj_dt_exec_object~get_parameters.

  CLEAR: et_parameter_def, et_parameter_val.

  CONSTANTS: lc_langu TYPE char5 VALUE 'SPRAS',
             lc_date  TYPE char4 VALUE 'DATS',
             lc_uom   TYPE char5 VALUE 'MEINS'.

  et_parameter_def = VALUE #(

    ( selname        = gv_date      kind           = if_apj_dt_exec_object=>parameter      datatype       = lc_date      length         = 20
      param_text     = 'Snapshot Date'
      changeable_ind = abap_true )

    ( selname        = gv_lang      kind           = if_apj_dt_exec_object=>parameter      datatype       = lc_langu      length         = 20
      param_text     = 'Language'
      changeable_ind = abap_true )

    ( selname        = gv_uom      kind           = if_apj_dt_exec_object=>parameter      datatype       = lc_uom      length         = 20
      param_text     = 'Unit of Measure'
      changeable_ind = abap_true )
  ).

ENDMETHOD.

Step 3 — GET_PARAMETERS : Select Options

 
 
abap
METHOD if_apj_dt_exec_object~get_parameters.

  CLEAR: et_parameter_def, et_parameter_val.

  CONSTANTS: lc_char  TYPE char8 VALUE 'CHAR30',
             lc_lngth TYPE int2  VALUE 50.

  et_parameter_def = VALUE #(

    ( selname        = gv_contracttype      kind           = if_apj_dt_exec_object=>select_option      datatype       = lc_char      length         = lc_lngth      component_type = 'TCTYP'
      param_text     = 'Contract Type'
      changeable_ind = abap_true )

    ( selname        = gv_compcode      kind           = if_apj_dt_exec_object=>select_option      datatype       = lc_char      length         = lc_lngth      component_type = 'BUKRS'
      param_text     = 'Company Code'
      changeable_ind = abap_true )

    ( selname        = gv_plant      kind           = if_apj_dt_exec_object=>select_option      datatype       = lc_char      length         = lc_lngth      component_type = 'WERKS_D'
      param_text     = 'Plant'
      changeable_ind = abap_true )
  ).

ENDMETHOD.

Step 4 — EXECUTE Method : Single Values

METHOD if_apj_rt_exec_object~execute.

  DATA: lv_date      TYPE dats,
        lv_lang      TYPE spras,
        lv_uom       TYPE meins,
        lv_text_item TYPE string,
        lv_string    TYPE string,
        lv_timestamp TYPE timestamp,
        lv_filename  TYPE string,
        lt_final_data TYPE TABLE OF string.

  " Read incoming parameters
  LOOP AT it_parameters INTO DATA(ls_param) WHERE low IS NOT INITIAL.
    CASE ls_param-selname.
      WHEN gv_date. lv_date = ls_param-low.
      WHEN gv_lang. lv_lang = ls_param-low.
      WHEN gv_uom.  lv_uom  = ls_param-low.
    ENDCASE.
  ENDLOOP.

  " Read from your CDS / DB view
  SELECT * FROM zcds_your_query_view(
                  p_date     = @lv_date,
                  p_language = @lv_lang,
                  p_uom      = @lv_uom )
    INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_results).

  " Build pipe-delimited output dynamically using RTTI
  LOOP AT lt_results INTO DATA(ls_row).
    CLEAR lv_text_item.
    DATA(lo_struct) = CAST cl_abap_structdescr(
                        cl_abap_typedescr=>describe_by_data( ls_row ) ).

    LOOP AT lo_struct->components INTO DATA(ls_comp).
      ASSIGN COMPONENT ls_comp-name OF STRUCTURE ls_row             TO FIELD-SYMBOL(<lfs_val>).
      IF <lfs_val> IS ASSIGNED.
        lv_string = CONV #( <lfs_val> ).
        IF lv_text_item IS INITIAL.
          lv_text_item = lv_string.
        ELSE.
          CONCATENATE lv_text_item lv_string            INTO lv_text_item SEPARATED BY '|'.
        ENDIF.
      ENDIF.
    ENDLOOP.

    APPEND lv_text_item TO lt_final_data.
  ENDLOOP.

  " Write output file
  GET TIME STAMP FIELD lv_timestamp.
  lv_filename = |ZREPORT_OUTPUT_{ lv_date }_{ lv_timestamp }|.

  IF lt_final_data IS NOT INITIAL.
    OPEN DATASET lv_filename FOR OUTPUT IN TEXT MODE ENCODING DEFAULT.
    LOOP AT lt_final_data INTO DATA(ls_line).
      TRANSFER ls_line TO lv_filename.
    ENDLOOP.
    CLOSE DATASET lv_filename.
  ENDIF.

ENDMETHOD.

Step 5 — EXECUTE Method : Select Options

 
 
METHOD if_apj_rt_exec_object~execute.

  DATA: lt_contract_type TYPE RANGE OF tctyp,
        lt_plant         TYPE RANGE OF werks_d,
        lt_company_code  TYPE RANGE OF bukrs,
        lv_where_clause  TYPE string,
        lv_text_header   TYPE string,
        lv_text_item     TYPE string,
        lv_filename      TYPE string,
        lt_final_data    TYPE TABLE OF string,
        lt_temp          TYPE dfies_tab.

  " Build WHERE clause dynamically from select options
  LOOP AT it_parameters INTO DATA(ls_param) WHERE low IS NOT INITIAL.
    CASE ls_param-selname.
      WHEN gv_contracttype.
        APPEND VALUE #( sign   = 'I'
                        option = ls_param-option                        low    = ls_param-low                        high   = ls_param-high ) TO lt_contract_type.
        lv_where_clause = COND #(
          WHEN lv_where_clause IS INITIAL
          THEN 'contracttype IN @lt_contract_type'
          ELSE lv_where_clause && ' AND contracttype IN @lt_contract_type' ).

      WHEN gv_compcode.
        APPEND VALUE #( sign   = 'I'
                        option = ls_param-option                        low    = ls_param-low                        high   = ls_param-high ) TO lt_company_code.
        lv_where_clause = COND #(
          WHEN lv_where_clause IS INITIAL
          THEN 'companycode IN @lt_company_code'
          ELSE lv_where_clause && ' AND companycode IN @lt_company_code' ).

      WHEN gv_plant.
        APPEND VALUE #( sign   = 'I'
                        option = ls_param-option                        low    = ls_param-low                        high   = ls_param-high ) TO lt_plant.
        lv_where_clause = COND #(
          WHEN lv_where_clause IS INITIAL
          THEN 'plant IN @lt_plant'
          ELSE lv_where_clause && ' AND plant IN @lt_plant' ).
    ENDCASE.
  ENDLOOP.

  " Select using dynamic WHERE clause
  SELECT * FROM zcds_your_position_view    WHERE (lv_where_clause)
    INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_position).

  IF sy-subrc = 0.
    " Get column headers via DDIF_FIELDINFO_GET
    CALL FUNCTION 'DDIF_FIELDINFO_GET'
      EXPORTING
        tabname        = 'ZCDS_YOUR_POSITION_VIEW'
        langu          = sy-langu      TABLES
        dfies_tab      = lt_temp      EXCEPTIONS
        not_found      = 1
        internal_error = 2
        OTHERS         = 3.

    " Build header row
    DATA(lt_columns) = VALUE string_table(
      FOR ls_f IN lt_temp INDEX INTO lv_idx      WHERE ( lv_idx > 1 ) " skip MANDT
      ( ls_f-fieldname ) ).

    LOOP AT lt_columns INTO DATA(lv_col).
      lv_text_header = COND #(
        WHEN lv_text_header IS INITIAL THEN lv_col        ELSE lv_text_header && '|' && lv_col ).
    ENDLOOP.

    " Build data rows
    LOOP AT lt_position INTO DATA(ls_pos).
      " Concatenate your fields with | separator
      CONCATENATE
        ls_pos-field1  ls_pos-field2  ls_pos-field3        " ... add all required fields
        INTO lv_text_item SEPARATED BY '|'.
      APPEND lv_text_item TO lt_final_data.
    ENDLOOP.

    " Insert header at top
    INSERT lv_text_header INTO lt_final_data INDEX 1.

    " Write to application server
    CONCATENATE '/usr/sap/trans/' sy-uname '_' sy-uzeit '.xls'
      INTO lv_filename.

    IF lt_final_data IS NOT INITIAL.
      OPEN DATASET lv_filename FOR OUTPUT IN TEXT MODE ENCODING DEFAULT.
      LOOP AT lt_final_data INTO DATA(ls_line).
        TRANSFER ls_line TO lv_filename.
      ENDLOOP.
      CLOSE DATASET lv_filename.
    ENDIF.
  ENDIF.

ENDMETHOD.

Step 6 — Create Job Catalog & Template in ADT

  1. In ADT (Eclipse) → New → Application Job Catalog Entry
    • Enter your class name (ZCL_MY_APJ_JOB)
    • Give it a Catalog Name (e.g. ZCAT_MY_JOB)
  2. New → Application Job Template
    • Reference the Catalog Name created above
    • Define default parameter values
  3. Schedule via Application Jobs Fiori app (transaction /n/SDF/JOBD or Fiori Launchpad)

entry.title: Disabling CSRF Token Validation in SAP for Testing with Postman and External Applications
entry.content:
Introduction

When working with SAP OData services, developers frequently encounter CSRF token validation errors while testing APIs using tools like Postman or integrating with third-party applications. These errors commonly occur during POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE operations because SAP Gateway enforces CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) protection for security purposes.

In this blog, we will walk through:

  • What CSRF token validation is in SAP
  • Why Postman and external applications face CSRF-related issues
  • How to disable CSRF token validation for a specific SAP OData service
  • Testing the service using SAP Gateway Client and Postman

What is CSRF Token Validation in SAP?

CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery) protection is a security mechanism implemented by SAP Gateway to prevent unauthorized requests from malicious applications.

For modifying operations such as:

  • POST
  • PUT
  • PATCH
  • DELETE

SAP requires a valid X-CSRF-Token header.

If the token is missing or invalid, SAP returns errors such as:

  • 403 Forbidden
  • CSRF token validation failed

This issue is very common while testing APIs from:

  • Postman
  • External middleware applications
  • Custom UI applications
  • Third-party integrations

Common Issue Faced in Postman

Most developers directly trigger a POST or PUT request from Postman without first fetching the CSRF token.

As a result, SAP Gateway rejects the request due to missing token validation.

Setting the value to 0 disables CSRF token validation for the service

Testing from Postman

After disabling CSRF validation, you can directly perform:

  • POST requests
  • PUT requests

Conclusion

Efficient API testing is essential for successful SAP integrations, and managing CSRF token validation is a key part of that process. Whether you are working with Postman, middleware platforms, or custom applications, knowing how to configure and troubleshoot CSRF settings can save considerable development time. Always ensure that any security relaxation performed for testing is carefully controlled and documented to avoid risks in productive environments.

entry.title: Sending HTML Notifications in SAP SRM Without SO10 — Using CL_BBP_DOC_SEND_BCS and OData
entry.content:
Why This Blog

While working on an SAP SRM workflow requirement, I needed to send HTML email notifications with a link back to the application. My first thought was to use SO10, but I didn't have the required authorization in that system. Instead, I explored using CL_BBP_DOC_SEND to generate the HTML directly in ABAP.

After implementing and testing this approach, I found that it worked well for scenarios where maintaining SO10 templates wasn't an option. Since I couldn't find much documentation on this specific approach in the SAP Community, I thought it would be useful to share the solution and the implementation steps.

1. Why Skip SO10 at All?

SO10 is still the first option I'd recommend for most notification templates because it's easy for functional teams to maintain and supports translations. In my case, I couldn't use it because I didn't have the required authorization, so I needed another solution.

I also found that when the email contains dynamic HTML and application links, most of the content still has to be built in ABAP. For this requirement, generating the HTML directly in code turned out to be a simpler approach.

2. Building the HTML Body Cleanly (String Templates, Not CONCATENATE Chains)

I initially considered using CONCATENATE statements, but the code quickly became difficult to read. String templates made the HTML much cleaner and easier to maintain, especially when inserting dynamic values like document numbers and links.

One small thing that took me a while to notice was escaping curly braces in CSS. If you're using string templates for HTML, this is something to watch out for.

DATA(lv_link) = |{ lv_base_url }&/YourEntitySet(DocumentGuid={ ls_notification-doc_guid })|.

DATA(lv_html) =
  |<html><head><meta http-equiv="Content-Type" content="text/html; charset=UTF-8">| &&
  |<style type="text/css">| &&
  |  body \{ background-color: #f4f8fc; \}| &&
  |  .ntable \{ font-family: Arial, sans-serif; color: #333333; width: 640px; | &&
  |             background-color: #FFFFFF; margin: 0 auto; border-collapse: collapse; \}| &&
  |  .ntable td \{ padding: 12px 24px; \}| &&
  |  .ntable a \{ color: #1565C0; font-weight: bold; \}| &&
  |</style></head><body>| &&
  |<table class="ntable">| &&
  |  <tr style="background-color:#0D47A1; color:#FFFFFF;">| &&
  |    <td><!-- Replace with your own hosted company logo --> Document Notification</td>| &&
  |  </tr>| &&
  |  <tr><td style="padding-top:20px;"><b>Dear Colleague,</b></td></tr>| &&
  |  <tr><td>| &&
  |    Your document <b>{ ls_notification-doc_id }</b> has been updated to status | &&
  |    <b>{ ls_notification-status_text }</b>.<br/><br/>| &&
  |    You can review the full details here: <a href="{ lv_link }">Open Document</a>.| &&
  |  </td></tr>| &&
  |  <tr><td style="padding-top:20px;">Best regards,<br/><b>Procurement System</b></td></tr>| &&
  |  <tr style="font-size:11px; color:#0D47A1; background-color:#E3F2FD;">| &&
  |    <td>Support: support@yourcompany.com | Internal Helpdesk: 1000</td>| &&
  |  </tr>| &&
  |</table></body></html>|.

Note the \{ / \} escaping — since curly braces are the string-template syntax marker, any literal {/} you need inside the HTML/CSS (like body { ... }) has to be escaped this way. This is the most common typo people hit the first time they convert a CONCATENATE-based HTML builder to string templates.

3. Building the OData V4 Deep Link Correctly

To avoid hardcoding URLs, I stored the application's base URL in TVARVC. That way, the same code works across development, QA, and production without any changes. Only the TVARVC value needs to be maintained for each system.

SELECT SINGLE low FROM tvarvc
  INTO @DATA(lv_base_url)
  WHERE name = 'Z_NOTIFICATION_APP_BASE_URL'
    AND type = 'P'.

This is what lets the exact same code work unchanged across dev, QA, and production — only the TVARVC entry changes per system, not the code.

4. Sending via CL_BBP_DOC_SEND_BCS — The SRM-Specific Mail Class

Since this requirement was part of an SAP SRM workflow, I preferred using CL_BBP_DOC_SEND_BCS instead of calling CL_BCS directly. It fits naturally with the SRM notification framework and worked well in my testing.

One thing worth checking is the mail format. If the format isn't set to 'HTM', the email may display the HTML tags instead of rendering them.

DATA: lt_body   TYPE bcsy_text,
      ls_body   TYPE soli,
      lv_xstring TYPE xstring,
      lv_output_done TYPE abap_bool.

ls_body-line = lv_html.
APPEND ls_body TO lt_body.

CALL METHOD cl_bbp_doc_send_bcs=>send_mail_cc
  EXPORTING
    iv_sender       = 'WF-BATCH'
    it_recipient    = lt_recipient
    iv_subject      = |Document { ls_notification-doc_id } - Status Updated|
    iv_mail_format  = 'HTM'
    iv_commit       = 'X'
    it_body         = lt_body
  IMPORTING
    ev_output_done  = lv_output_done
  EXCEPTIONS
    error_mail_send = 1
    OTHERS          = 2.

IF sy-subrc <> 0.
  " Log to application log (SLG1) rather than letting this fail silently in a background job
  MESSAGE ID sy-msgid TYPE 'E' NUMBER sy-msgno
    WITH sy-msgv1 sy-msgv2 sy-msgv3 sy-msgv4
    INTO DATA(lv_dummy).
ENDIF.

5. Codepage Conversion — Don't Skip This If You Have Any Non-ASCII Content

If your email contains special characters or multiple languages, it's a good idea to convert the content to UTF-8. I included this step to avoid character encoding issues in different email clients.

lv_xstring = cl_abap_codepage=>convert_to(
               source   = lv_html
               codepage = 'UTF-8' ).

6. When to Still Reach for SO10 (or CDS Email Templates) Instead

Although this approach solved my requirement, I wouldn't use it for every scenario. If functional users need to update the email content regularly or multiple languages have to be maintained, SO10 or the newer email template framework is still the better long-term choice.

For my case, the email content was developer-owned and changed rarely, so keeping it in ABAP was acceptable.

7. Summary

This solution worked well for my SRM requirement and gave me a way to generate HTML notifications without depending on SO10. If you're in a similar situation, I hope this approach saves you some implementation time.

entry.title: Managing Contract Attachments in SAP SRM Using OData Service
entry.content:
Introduction

 

 

While developing a Fiori application for SAP SRM Contract management, one of the requirements was to allow users to maintain contract attachments without opening SAP GUI.

The users wanted to perform the following operations directly from the application:

  • Upload a new attachment to an SRM Contract
  • Update the description of an existing attachment
  • Delete an existing attachment

The frontend application sends the uploaded file as a Base64 string, whereas the SAP SRM attachment framework expects the file content in binary format along with additional metadata such as GUID, MIME type, description, and visibility.

In this blog, I will explain how I implemented contract attachment management using a custom OData service and standard SAP SRM function modules.

Business Scenario

Consider a user working with an SRM Contract from a Fiori application.

The user uploads a new file, for example:

Contract_Amendment.pdf

The file is sent from the frontend as Base64 content.

The OData service receives this request, converts the file into the required format, prepares the attachment structure, updates the contract, validates the changes, and finally saves the attachment against the SRM Contract.

The same service is also used when the user wants to update an attachment description or remove an attachment.

Reading the Existing Document

Before making any changes, I first read the document along with its existing attachments.

CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PROCDOC_GETDETAIL_DIRECT'
  EXPORTING
    i_object_id   = lv_documentnumber
    i_object_type = gc_obj_bus2000113
    i_read_flags  = ls_read_flags
  IMPORTING
    e_header      = ls_header
    et_attach     = et_attach.

Here, BUS2000113 represents the SRM Contract object type.

Initially, I thought only the contract header information would be required. However, during testing, I realized that all attachment operations depend on the existing attachment collection.

The attachment table returned by this function is used as the base for:

  • Adding a new attachment
  • Updating an existing attachment description
  • Marking an attachment for deletion

Handling Multiple Operations with a Single Service

Instead of creating separate OData operations for upload, delete, and update, I used a single CREATE_ENTITY implementation.

The action received from the frontend determines which operation needs to be executed.

CASE ls_create-action.

  WHEN 'UPLOAD'.

  WHEN 'DELETE'.

  WHEN 'EDITDESC'.

ENDCASE.

This keeps both the frontend and backend simple. The frontend only calls one endpoint, and the backend decides which logic to execute.

Uploading the Attachment

When the file reaches the backend, it is still in Base64 format.

The first thing I do is convert it into an XSTRING.

DATA(lv_xstring_content) =
    cl_http_utility=>decode_x_base64(
        encoded = ls_create-filebase64 ).

The attachment framework cannot directly save Base64 data, so this conversion is mandatory.

Once the content is available, I generate a new GUID for the attachment.

CALL FUNCTION 'GUID_CREATE'

The GUID uniquely identifies the attachment inside the SRM document.

Why the MIME Type Is Important

One issue I encountered during testing was that some uploaded files were not recognized correctly when the MIME type was missing.

Instead of assigning a fixed value, I extract the file extension from the uploaded filename and determine the MIME type dynamically.

CALL FUNCTION 'SDOK_MIMETYPE_GET'

If no MIME type is returned, I assign application/pdf as a fallback.

This small check prevented several upload issues during testing.

Preparing the File for SRM

Although the file is now available as an XSTRING, the SRM attachment framework expects binary content.

For that reason, I convert it before appending it to the attachment table.

CALL FUNCTION 'SCMS_XSTRING_TO_BINARY'

After the conversion, I populate the remaining attachment fields and append the new attachment to the existing attachment collection.

At this point, nothing has been saved yet. The attachment is only prepared for the update process.

Updating or Deleting an Existing Attachment

For updating the description, I simply locate the attachment using its GUID and change the description field.

<fs_attach>-description = ls_create-description.

Deleting an attachment works a little differently.

Initially, I expected to remove the entry from the internal table. After checking how the SRM framework works, I found that SAP only expects the deletion indicator to be set.

<fs_attach>-del_ind = abap_true.

The framework removes the attachment automatically when the contract is saved.

Updating the Document

Once the attachment table reflects the required changes, I pass it to the contract update API.

CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PD_CTR_UPDATE'

This prepares the modified contract, but it does not immediately write anything to the database.

Before saving, I validate the contract.

CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PD_CTR_CHECK'

Only if no validation errors are returned do I proceed with the save.

CALL FUNCTION 'BBP_PD_CTR_SAVE'.

COMMIT WORK AND WAIT.

This sequence ensures that attachment changes are saved only when the contract is in a consistent state.

The interesting part of this implementation was that the actual upload logic was only a small portion of the solution. Most of the work involved understanding how the SRM attachment framework expects attachment data to be prepared before it can be saved.

Using a single OData service for upload, delete, and description updates helped keep the implementation straightforward, while the standard SRM function modules handled the actual persistence and validation.

If you're implementing a similar requirement in SAP SRM, I hope this walkthrough gives you a good starting point.
